opus-5.5.text:
Honestly, the first thing I look at is not how many features it has, but whether it gets out of the model's way. A lot of agent frameworks were designed when models were weaker, so they're full of hand-written workflows, rigid planning steps, lots of prompt scaffolding. That made sense back then, but as the base model gets stronger, all that structure can start to become a ceiling instead of a support. So I ask: if the model gets twice as capable next year, does this framework let that capability show up, or does it lock the model into yesterday's way of thinking?

The second thing is the environment and the tools. An agent is only as good as what it can actually touch and observe. Is the tool interface clean? Is the feedback from the environment real and informative, or is it noisy and lossy? Can the model see the actual result of its actions and correct itself? For me, the quality of that feedback loop matters more than clever orchestration on top.

Third, I care a lot about context management over long tasks. Real tasks aren't five steps; they're hundreds of steps, hours of work. How does the framework handle memory, summarization, picking up where it left off? A lot of systems look great in a demo and then fall apart at step fifty because the context gets polluted or the model loses track of the goal.

And finally, from a research perspective, I look at whether it's trainable. Can the trajectories it produces be used to improve the model? Is it consistent enough between how we evaluate, how we do reinforcement learning, and how users actually use it? If the training environment and the real product environment are very different, you end up optimizing for the wrong thing. The best frameworks, in my view, are simple, close to the real environment, and grow together with the model rather than compensating for it.

fable-5.1.text:
When I look at an agent framework, the first thing I ask is: how much does it get out of the way? A lot of frameworks look impressive in a demo because they bundle planning, memory, tool calling, reflection, all these modules. But every layer of abstraction is a layer between the model and the actual problem. If the model is strong, most of that scaffolding becomes a constraint rather than a help. So I look at whether the framework lets the model's capability show through, or whether it's really compensating for a weak model.

The second thing is the interface to the environment. The quality of an agent is largely determined by what it can observe and what it can act on. If the tool abstraction is leaky, if the error messages are swallowed, if the state isn't visible, the agent is working blind. I care more about clean, honest feedback loops than about clever orchestration logic.

Third, and this is where I'm probably more opinionated: can you train through it? For me the real question isn't just whether the framework runs an agent, it's whether the trajectories it produces are usable for improving the model. Is the logging complete, is it reproducible, can you plug a reward signal in. A framework that's only a runtime is a dead end. A framework that's also a data engine is where the compounding happens.

And then honestly, the last thing is simplicity. If I can't read the core loop in an afternoon and understand exactly what the model sees at each step, I don't trust it. Agents fail in subtle ways, and you need to be able to trace it back.
